svg.title: Apache Cassandra
svg.desc: Apache Cassandra. A wide-column database built for heavy writes across data centres: a token ring, tunable consistency and LSM storage. Step 1, Where it sits: Both data centres take writes for every parcel; each serves its own customers, with no primary. Step 2, Partition and replicate: S-77 hashes into bkk-2's range; the write goes to every replica, and LOCAL_QUORUM acks at 2 of 3. Step 3, Inside a node: bkk-2 logs the write, adds it to the memtable; a read merges memtable and SSTables; files compact. Step 4, Failure and the limits: bkk-3 is down: 2 of 3 still ack and a hint waits. Limits: query-first tables, big partitions, LWTs.

g.text: Both data centres take writes for every parcel; each serves its own customers, with no primary.
S-77 hashes into bkk-2's range; the write goes to every replica, and LOCAL_QUORUM acks at 2 of 3.
bkk-2 logs the write, adds it to the memtable; a read merges memtable and SSTables; files compact.
bkk-3 is down: 2 of 3 still ack and a hint waits. Limits: query-first tables, big partitions, LWTs.
keyspace tracking · NetworkTopologyStrategy: 3 replicas in dc-bkk, 3 in dc-sgp · reads and writes at LOCAL_QUORUM
SELECT * FROM shipment_events WHERE shipment_id = 'S-77' LIMIT 10
both DCs hold every row; customers read the top (LIMIT 10)
Parcels produce status events, millions a day, in Bangkok and Singapore. Each data centre serves its own clients and holds a full copy;
every node takes reads and writes, so there is no primary to fail over. One partition per shipment keeps its events together, newest first.
coordinator: bkk-1, the node the request reached
tokens run from −2⁶³ to 2⁶³−1; this one falls in bkk-2's range (sgp-2's in dc-sgp)
each node owns 16 small ranges (num_tokens: 16), drawn here as one
replicas: walk the ring clockwise from the token to 3 distinct nodes per DC
with 3 nodes and RF 3 each node holds every partition; a bigger DC picks 3
LOCAL_QUORUM: answer once 2 of the 3 replicas in dc-bkk have it
R + W > RF: 2 + 2 > 3, so a LOCAL_QUORUM read in dc-bkk sees the write
Murmur3 turns the partition key S-77 into a token; walking the ring clockwise from it gives the 3 replicas in each data centre.
A write always goes to every replica. LOCAL_QUORUM answers after 2 of the 3 in dc-bkk; dc-sgp gets it too, without the client waiting.
SELECT * FROM shipment_events WHERE shipment_id = 'S-77' LIMIT 10
one replica's storage engine, a log-structured merge tree
memtable · in memory, sorted by key
flushed: empty again, takes the next writes
bloom filter: could S-77 be in this file?
the next flush becomes a new SSTable here
read: 5 rows, newest first · the tombstone hides the 22:10 row
compaction merged SSTables 1 and 3 into 5 in the background; the tombstone stays
INSIDE A NODE: COMMIT LOG, MEMTABLE, SSTABLES
A write is appended to the commit log and added to the memtable, then acknowledged. Full memtables are flushed to immutable SSTables.
A read merges the memtable with the SSTables whose bloom filter says maybe. A DELETE writes a tombstone; compaction merges SSTables.
what decides when to choose something else
every query names the partition key; no joins;
a huge partition or a pile of tombstones slows
IF NOT EXISTS runs Paxos: 4 round trips
repair, compaction, upgrades and capacity are yours
5.0 (Sept 2024): SAI indexes, vector search, trie memtables and SSTables, UCS
general transactions (Accord) are in 6.0, an alpha release as of October 2026
bkk-3 is down, yet bkk-1 and bkk-2 make 2 of 3, so the write succeeds. bkk-1 keeps a hint and replays it when bkk-3 is back.
Hints are written only for the first max_hint_window of an outage (3 h by default); after that, repair. Repair every node within gc_grace_seconds.
